quiz.q: What is the default visibility of an item in Rust?
options: pub
Private, scoped to its defining module and that module's descendants
pub(crate)
Depends on the file name
quiz.explain: Every item is private by default — visible only within the module that defines it and that module's descendant modules.

quiz.q: What does `pub(crate)` expose that plain `pub` doesn't restrict?
options: Nothing different — they're identical
Visibility across your whole crate, but not to downstream users of a published crate
Visibility to just the parent module
Visibility only within the same file
quiz.explain: pub(crate) is visible everywhere inside the crate, but external crates using this one as a library still can't see it — unlike plain pub.

options: The entire crate
Just the immediate parent module
Only the same module
Every module except the parent
quiz.explain: pub(super) exposes an item to the module one level up (the parent), and no further.

quiz.q: If `Account` is a `pub` struct, are its fields automatically `pub` too?
options: Yes, always
No — each field needs its own pub marker
Only the first declared field is pub
Only if the struct derives Debug
quiz.explain: A pub struct's fields stay private by default; visibility is decided field by field, independent of the struct's own visibility.

options: Makes an entire module public
Re-exports an item under a new path, so callers don't need to know your internal module layout
Deletes the original item definition
Only works for functions, not types
quiz.explain: pub use re-exports an item (often flattening a deep internal path into a short public one) without moving the original definition.

quiz.q: Why can't outside code write `inventory::Item { name: ..., price: ... }` if `Item`'s `name` field is private?
options: Struct literals never work outside the defining crate
A struct literal must set every field, and outside code can't set a private field
price must also be private for this to matter
Item needs #[derive(Default)] first
quiz.explain: Struct literal syntax needs to set every field; a private field can't be set from outside its module, so outside code needs a public constructor function instead.

quiz.q: Why is defaulting to the narrowest visibility (rather than always using pub) usually the better choice?
options: It compiles faster
Every pub item is a permanent promise to callers — widening later is easy, narrowing is a breaking change
Rust limits how many pub items a module can have
pub items use more memory at runtime
quiz.explain: Once something is pub, external code may depend on it; narrowing visibility later breaks that code, so it's safer to start narrow and widen only when genuinely needed.

quiz.q: Does Rust's privacy system follow file boundaries or module boundaries?
options: File boundaries — each file is its own privacy scope
Module boundaries — modules can span multiple files or share one file
Both equally
Neither — privacy only applies per-crate
quiz.explain: Privacy is entirely about the module tree; how you split modules across files has no effect on visibility rules.

flashcards.front: What is Rust's default visibility for items?
flashcards.back: Private — visible only to the defining module and its descendant modules.
Visible anywhere inside the current crate, but invisible to downstream users if this crate is published as a library.
Visible to just the immediate parent module, one level up — and no further.

flashcards.front: Does making a struct pub make its fields pub?
flashcards.back: No — each field's visibility is set independently of the struct's own visibility.
Re-exports an item under a new path so callers don't need to know (or depend on) your internal module layout.

flashcards.front: Why can't you build a struct literal for a type with a private field, from outside its module?
flashcards.back: A struct literal must set every field, and private fields can't be set from outside — you need a public constructor instead.

flashcards.front: What's the risk of marking everything pub "to be safe"?
flashcards.back: Every pub item becomes a permanent part of your public API — widening later is easy, narrowing is a breaking change.

flashcards.front: Does Rust privacy follow files or modules?
flashcards.back: Modules — file layout has no bearing on visibility rules.
